design_detail: Prospective 24-month, three-arm, parallel randomized trial in Hong Kong (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03485417) of aripiprazole or paliperidone, started early and titrated to schizophrenia treatment doses (oral or long-acting injection), against treatment as usual (TAU: the treating psychiatrist's choice, with or without another antipsychotic) in 165 people aged 16 to 50 with DSM-5 stimulant-induced psychosis (methamphetamine or cocaine), randomized 1:1:2. Two phases: months 0 to 12 with outcome assessors blinded to allocation (participants and prescribers not blinded); months 12 to 24 open-label, with assessors unblinded and participants free to continue or stop their assigned treatment. Primary outcomes as published: change in CGI-S, CGI-I and CGI-E at 12 months (primary endpoint) and 24 months (secondary endpoint), by mixed models for repeated measures in the intention-to-treat sample. Read: the full article on the publisher's site, including Tables 1 to 3 (rendered as text), the data, ethics, author-contribution, funding, acknowledgement and conflict-of-interest statements and the reference list; Figures 1 to 3 (assessment schedule, CONSORT diagram, CGI change plots) are images and their values were not extracted; Supplementary Tables S1 to S12 and Figures S1 and S2 were not read. Registration, outcome and eligibility history additionally read from the ClinicalTrials.gov record (current version and record versions 7, 13, 14 and 15).
can_establish: Whether, in this Hong Kong sample with mostly mild stimulant-induced psychosis, randomization to protocolized aripiprazole or paliperidone was followed by better clinician-rated global outcomes than usual care over 12 and 24 months, within the limits set by a primary outcome changed after data collection, heavy attrition and an unblinded second year.
cannot_establish: Whether antipsychotics help more than no antipsychotic or than abstinence (usual care included antipsychotics for 45% of its participants at randomization and for most by 24 months, and there was no placebo), whether they prevent relapse (the registered primary outcome, which is not reported) or conversion to schizophrenia (7 conversions among 137 people), or what happens in methamphetamine psychosis as distinct from cocaine psychosis or primary psychosis (17% had an earlier schizophrenia or schizoaffective diagnosis).

sample.recruitment: Community services, specialized substance-misuse clinics, and general psychiatric and medical wards and clinics in Hong Kong, described as random sampling; assessments at four outpatient psychiatric centres; recruitment from 1 June 2019 to May 2022 and final follow-up on 31 May 2024; USD 25 per completed follow-up assessment (2.1 Study design and participants, 2nd paragraph; 2.4 Outcome assessments, 2nd paragraph; 3 Results, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Methods).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Age 16 to 50, stimulants as the primary drug, and stimulant-induced psychotic symptoms, with DSM-5 diagnosis confirmed by a psychiatrist; detailed criteria only in Supplementary Table S1, not read (2.1, 2nd paragraph; 2.4, 2nd paragraph). The registry excludes, among others, people diagnosed with schizophrenia, another substance-induced psychotic or mood disorder, bipolar disorder or psychotic depression, and people in remission on maintenance antipsychotics (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03485417, Eligibility Criteria). A post hoc review of electronic health records found 28 participants (5 aripiprazole, 11 paliperidone, 12 TAU) with a diagnosis of schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder before enrolment (3.6 Conversion from StIP to schizophrenia).
sample.demographics: Mean age 38.69 (SD 10.08); 69.70% men; 89.70% had ever used methamphetamine (more than 70% in the 3 months before enrolment) and 59.39% cocaine, 49.70% both; mean duration of methamphetamine use 125.21 months; tobacco 90.18%, alcohol 70.30%, lifetime cannabis 74.55% and ketamine 60.00%; forensic history 63.64%; earlier psychiatric inpatient care 70.91%. Baseline CGI-S 3.33 (1.29) and BPRS-24 29.70 (6.00), which the authors describe as mildly ill; 105 of 160 baseline urine samples (65.63%) were stimulant-positive (3.1 Baseline characteristics; Table 1; 4 Discussion, 2nd paragraph). The aripiprazole arm had fewer men (45.24% vs 82.50% on paliperidone and 75.90% on TAU), was younger (34.36 vs 39.95 and 40.28 years) and had higher BPRS-24 (31.55 vs 28.33 on TAU) and Severity of Dependence Scale scores (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Assessments were completed by 70.30% (116 of 165) at 12 months and 53.94% (89 of 165) at 24 months, said not to differ significantly between groups (Supplementary Table S3, not read) (3 Results, 1st paragraph). The responder-analysis denominators imply 24 of 42 (57%), 28 of 40 (70%) and 64 of 83 (77%) assessed at 12 months, and 21 (50%), 18 (45%) and 50 (60%) at 24 months (Table 3; editors' calculation; chi-square for 12 months 5.3 on 2 df, p = 0.07). The CONSORT diagram (Figure 2) is an image and was not read.
sample.selection_effects: A treatment-engaged Hong Kong sample with mostly mild psychosis (mean CGI-S about 3) and moderate stimulant use disorder, which the authors say limits extrapolation to severe presentations (4.1 Strengths and limitations, 2nd paragraph); 17% had an earlier primary psychotic diagnosis; about 10% had never used methamphetamine (cocaine-induced psychosis).

exposure.measurement: Study medication dispensed through three hospital pharmacies; adherence to oral medication from dispensing records and psychiatrists' reports; long-acting injections given on site by nurses independent of the study team (2.3 Medications, 2nd paragraph). Stimulant use by urine drug testing and by the SCID-5-CV, the Severity of Dependence Scale and the Addiction Severity Index (2.4, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: a 1-week lead-in at the lowest oral dose (aripiprazole 2 mg/day, paliperidone 3 mg/day), titration over 3 weeks by clinical response, then maintenance within the range recommended for schizophrenia, orally or as a long-acting injection (2.3, 1st paragraph). Mean oral-equivalent doses were 15 mg/day (range 2 to 30) for aripiprazole and 8.1 mg/day (3 to 12) for paliperidone; 3 participants received aripiprazole and 10 paliperidone as long-acting injections (3.2 Medications and safety, 1st paragraph). TAU: routine treatment chosen by the attending psychiatrist under UK guidance, with no antipsychotic or any antipsychotic other than the two study drugs; 55.43% of the TAU group were antipsychotic-free at baseline, 31.33% at 12 months and 24.10% at 24 months (2.3, 1st paragraph; 3.2, 1st paragraph). In months 12 to 24, two participants stopped aripiprazole, two switched from paliperidone to quetiapine or olanzapine and one added risperidone (3.2, 1st paragraph). No participant received structured psychotherapy or drug counselling (3 Results, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Lifetime use of cannabis, ketamine, MDMA, zopiclone, heroin, nimetazepam, midazolam and methadone recorded at baseline and similar across arms (Table 1); non-stimulant urine results compared between groups in Supplementary Table S11 (not read); other substance use not adjusted for in the analyses.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not required. 65.63% of baseline urine samples were stimulant-positive; at 24 months, 76.47% on paliperidone and 46.81% on TAU (3.1; 3.4 Secondary outcomes, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: Treatment as usual (83 randomized): the attending psychiatrist's routine treatment, which could include no antipsychotic or any antipsychotic except aripiprazole or paliperidone (2.3, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Randomized 1:1:2 with opaque sealed envelopes drawn from an opaque box by an independent staff member and handed to the attending psychiatrist (2.2 Randomization and blinding, 1st paragraph); how the sequence was generated is not described. Baseline differences in sex, age, forensic history, hospitalizations, drinking years, BPRS-24, Severity of Dependence Scale, ASI psychiatric status and lifetime use of both stimulants are flagged in Table 1; editors' chi-square for sex across the three arms 16.5 on 2 df, p < 0.001.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Family history of psychosis, earlier episodes of stimulant psychosis and the duration of the index episode are not reported in the article; earlier primary psychotic diagnoses were identified only after the trial, by record review.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Lifetime use of other substances was similar across arms (Table 1).

outcomes.instruments: Primary: Clinical Global Impression severity (CGI-S), improvement (CGI-I) and efficacy index (CGI-E). Secondary: BPRS-24, Glasgow Antipsychotic Side-effect Scale (GASS), SCID-5-CV severity of stimulant use disorder, Severity of Dependence Scale, SOCRATES-D, urine drug testing, MoCA, Frontal Assessment Battery and Addiction Severity Index; conversion to schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder by ICD-10, determined by the attending psychiatrist (2.4, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 2.5 Statistical analysis, 6th paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: CGI-I and CGI-E have no pre-randomization baseline (2.5, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, footnote b). The CGI-E combines a treatment's therapeutic effect with its side effects (registry description, scored 1 to 16); how it was scored for TAU participants taking no antipsychotic is not described. The BPRS-24 has a lowest possible score of 24 (registry description), so the baseline mean of 29.70 is close to the floor.
outcomes.operationalization: Primary estimand: change from baseline at each time point, by MMRM with treatment, time, baseline and their interactions, TAU as the reference; Cohen's d = group contrast divided by the model residual SD (2.5, 2nd paragraph). Responders: CGI-S of 3 or less, CGI-I of 3 or less, or a reduction of at least 50% in BPRS-24 total score from baseline (2.5, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for the three primary CGI scales, the two contrasts with TAU and the two time points. Secondary outcomes are called exploratory and not adjusted (2.5, 2nd paragraph). Bonferroni correction was applied to the responder chi-squares (alpha 0.0167) and to some side-effect comparisons (Table 3 footnote; 3.2, 2nd paragraph). Editors' count of 13: three primary scales and ten secondary outcomes.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Months 0 to 12: independent assessors blinded to allocation; prescribers did not rate their own patients; participants were asked not to reveal their treatment; blinding integrity was not assessed. Months 12 to 24: all assessors unblinded, and attending psychiatrists could rate patients they had treated (2.2, 2nd paragraph). The outcome-assessment section also names three authors as the psychiatrists who confirmed diagnoses and rated the CGI scales and BPRS-24 (2.4, 2nd paragraph), without saying at which visits.

analysis.effect_sizes: MMRM contrasts with TAU in change from baseline (Table 2). CGI-S at 12 months: aripiprazole −0.55 (95% CI −1.03 to −0.07), p = 0.03, d = −0.31; paliperidone −0.4 (−0.86 to 0.06), p = 0.09, d = −0.23; aripiprazole vs paliperidone −0.15 (−0.7 to 0.41). CGI-S at 24 months: aripiprazole −0.65 (−1.22 to −0.09), p = 0.03, d = −0.38; paliperidone −0.02 (−0.6 to 0.56), p = 0.94; aripiprazole vs paliperidone −0.63 (−1.31 to 0.05), p = 0.07. CGI-I at 12 months: aripiprazole −0.82 (−1.41 to −0.23), d = −0.45; paliperidone −0.94 (−1.49 to −0.4), d = −0.51; at 24 months aripiprazole −0.74 (−1.43 to −0.06), p = 0.04, d = −0.40; paliperidone 0.58 (−0.12 to 1.28), p = 0.11; aripiprazole vs paliperidone −1.32 (−2.15 to −0.5), d = −0.72. CGI-E at 12 months: aripiprazole −4.19 (−6.58 to −1.8), d = −1.72; paliperidone −3.3 (−5.47 to −1.14), d = −1.36; at 24 months aripiprazole −4.17 (−6.73 to −1.6), d = −1.71; paliperidone −1.23 (−3.74 to 1.29), p = 0.34. Responders (Table 3): CGI-S of 3 or less at 12 months in 70.83%, 75.0% and 64.06% (no significant differences); CGI-I of 3 or less at 12 months aripiprazole 15 of 24 (printed 71.43%), paliperidone 20 of 28 (71.43%), TAU 16 of 64 (25%), both active arms p ≤ 0.001 against TAU; BPRS-24 halved at 12 months in 16 of 24 (66.67%) on aripiprazole against 19 of 64 (29.69%) on TAU, p = 0.002; no significant responder difference at 24 months. Secondary (exploratory): no consistent between-group difference on BPRS-24 or the other measures; paliperidone against TAU at 24 months, stimulant-positive urine 76.47% vs 46.81%, OR 14.51 (2.07 to 101.74), and MoCA −2.06 (−3.28 to −0.85), d = −0.97 (3.4). Editors' check: the CGI p values agree with their intervals; the d values imply residual SDs of about 1.7 to 1.8 points for CGI-S and CGI-I and 2.4 for CGI-E.
analysis.covariates: Baseline value of the outcome where one exists, time and their interactions; no adjustment for the baseline imbalances in sex, age or symptom severity (2.5, 2nd paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03485417, first submitted 14 March 2018 and first posted 2 April 2018, before enrolment began on 1 June 2019. In version 7 (26 April 2019) and unchanged through version 13 (4 July 2025), the primary outcome was the relative risk of psychosis relapse over 36 months, with transition to schizophrenia (DSM-5) at 36 months and stimulant use disorder, MoCA and ASI-lite at 12 and 36 months as secondary outcomes. After the trial ended (primary completion 31 May 2024; study completion 31 May 2025), version 14 (12 November 2025) made the BPRS-24 at 12 and 24 months the primary outcome and, in the same update, shortened every registered time frame from 36 to 24 months, and version 15 (23 March 2026) replaced it with the CGI scales at 12 and 24 months, moving the BPRS-24 to secondary. Outcome measures changed only in versions 2, 14 and 15, so no 24-month design was registered before the outcome change. The registry's study completion (31 May 2025) is a year after the article's final follow-up (31 May 2024); neither source says whether any data were collected after 24 months. The article reports the CGI scales as primary, does not report relapse, and does not mention the changes. Registered masking: single (outcome assessor). The sample-size target of 240 (2.5, 1st paragraph) is not given in the registry, which records the actual enrolment of 165.
analysis.selective_reporting: The registered primary outcome (relapse over 36 months) is not reported. The primary outcome was changed twice after the data were collected, finishing on the CGI scales, on which aripiprazole differed from usual care, rather than the BPRS-24, which showed no consistent difference. Most secondary results are only in unread supplements; the text reports selected ones (stimulant urine tests and MoCA for paliperidone).
analysis.power: Target 240 participants to detect medium effect sizes (alpha 0.05, power 0.80), based on a trial of aripiprazole in amphetamine dependence; 165 were randomized (69% of the target) because of COVID-19 disruption (2.5, 1st paragraph; 3 Results, 1st paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: On clinician-rated global scales, aripiprazole improved more than usual care at 12 months (CGI-S difference −0.55 points, d −0.31) and at 24 months, when ratings were no longer blind; paliperidone improved CGI-I and CGI-E but not CGI-S at 12 months and nothing at 24 months. Psychotic symptoms on the BPRS-24 did not differ consistently, CGI-S responder rates did not differ, and without the 28 participants with an earlier schizophrenia or schizoaffective diagnosis the 12-month CGI-S difference was not significant (p = 0.12). Seven of 137 people (5.1%) were newly diagnosed with schizophrenia within 24 months, with no difference between arms.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions state that aripiprazole showed consistently favourable CGI-based outcomes and was well tolerated compared with usual care over 24 months, while paliperidone had more limited long-term benefit and may worsen stimulant use and cognition (Abstract › Conclusion; 4.2 Conclusions). Gaps: (1) the primary outcome reported is not the registered one (relapse over 36 months); it was changed after the trial ended, and the change is not disclosed; (2) 'consistent' sits beside no consistent difference in BPRS-24 symptoms, no difference in CGI-S responders, and a 12-month CGI-S effect that is not significant once participants who should have been ineligible (earlier schizophrenia) are excluded, which the discussion itself acknowledges (4 Discussion, 1st paragraph); (3) the 24-month benefits come from unblinded ratings; the abstract's methods say the assessors were unblinded after 12 months and the limitations ask for caution (4.1, 2nd paragraph), but the abstract's results and conclusion present the 24-month benefits without that caveat; (4) 'well tolerated' is said of the arm with the trial's only death, a suicide 6 months after randomization (not attributed to the drug); (5) the paliperidone harms on urine tests and cognition are exploratory, uncorrected secondary results, and the urine odds ratio's interval (2.07 to 101.74) implies p of about 0.007 rather than the printed p < 0.001; (6) the introduction says the 2021 network meta-analysis demonstrated that olanzapine and quetiapine are superior to risperidone, paliperidone or aripiprazole, although those estimates were indirect and rated low certainty (1 Introduction, 3rd paragraph). Against this, the abstract calls for large placebo-controlled trials, and the limitations name the missing placebo group, the heterogeneous usual care and the open second year.

timeline.event: Three-arm trial of aripiprazole, methylphenidate and placebo in amphetamine dependence (Tiihonen et al.), on which this trial's sample-size estimate was based (2.5, 1st paragraph).

One-year comparison of long-acting aripiprazole and paliperidone in comorbid psychosis and substance use disorder (Cuomo et al.), cited as concurring with the sustained aripiprazole benefit (4 Discussion, 1st paragraph).
Systematic review of six short randomized trials of antipsychotics in amphetamine psychosis
Network meta-analysis of six short head-to-head trials in methamphetamine psychosis, none with a placebo or usual-care arm

Systematic review of antipsychotic drug, dose and duration after amphetamine- and cannabis-induced psychosis, searched to 25 March 2026, before this trial was published; it found no trial that followed participants after antipsychotics were stopped
This trial: by the authors' account the first and longest randomized comparison of aripiprazole, paliperidone and usual care in stimulant-induced psychosis (4.1, 1st paragraph).

replication.where_it_stands: The only randomized comparison of antipsychotics against usual care in stimulant-induced psychosis found so far, and the longest trial; unreplicated. Because its primary outcome was changed after the data were collected, its CGI results are best read as exploratory until an independent trial with a pre-specified, blinded primary outcome tests them.

funding.funder: HKSAR Beat Drugs Fund, grant BDF180059; the acknowledgements thank the Beat Drugs Fund Association of the Narcotics Division, Security Bureau of the HKSAR, for funding the study (Funding; Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that the work was conducted without commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest (Conflict of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Department of Psychiatry, Li Ka Shing Faculty of Medicine, The University of Hong Kong, and the Department of Psychiatry, North District Hospital, Hospital Authority, Hong Kong. Three authors confirmed the diagnoses and rated the CGI scales and BPRS-24 (2.4, 2nd paragraph); the first author also did the formal analysis and acquired the funding (Author contributions). Study drugs were supplied through hospital pharmacies; no manufacturer involvement is reported.

what_would_settle_it: A double-blind trial in people with methamphetamine-induced psychosis, with eligibility checked against health records for earlier primary psychoses, comparing an antipsychotic with placebo or antipsychotic-free care on top of the same psychosocial treatment, with a pre-registered primary outcome (time to remission, or relapse after the drug is withdrawn), blinded assessment throughout, urine-verified use, and analyses that address dropout.

domains.note: Opaque envelopes drawn by independent staff suggest concealed allocation, but how the sequence was generated is not described and the envelopes are not described as numbered. The arms differ on sex more than chance readily explains (45% vs 83% vs 76% men; editors' chi-square p < 0.001) and also on age and baseline symptom severity.

Participants and prescribers knew the allocation; usual care was heterogeneous and changed over time (antipsychotic-free 55% at baseline, 31% at 12 months); concomitant medication was not controlled. The intention-to-treat MMRM is appropriate for the effect of assignment.

Only 70% were assessed at 12 months and 54% at 24 months, apparently fewer on aripiprazole (57% at 12 months) than on usual care (77%) by the responder denominators. The MMRM assumes data missing at random, no analysis of informative dropout is reported, and in psychosis whether people return for assessment plausibly depends on how they are.

Judged for CGI-S at 12 months: a subjective global rating by assessors blinded to allocation, but blinding was not checked, participants knew their treatment and side effects can reveal it. For CGI-I and CGI-E (no baseline; CGI-E undefined without a drug) and for all 24-month ratings (unblinded, with treating psychiatrists rating their own patients) this domain would be high.

The registered primary outcome (relapse over 36 months) is not reported; the primary outcome was changed after the data were collected, first to the BPRS-24 and then to the CGI scales on which aripiprazole differed from usual care; three CGI scales, two contrasts and two time points were reported without correction.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High risk of bias overall, from the selection of the reported result (a primary outcome changed after data collection, with the registered outcome unreported) and from missing outcome data (30% missing at 12 months and 46% at 24 months, apparently unequal between arms). The 24-month results carry the further risk of unblinded ratings by treating psychiatrists. The trial may be cited as the only randomized comparison with usual care, for its design, its serious adverse events and its count of conversions to schizophrenia; its CGI advantage for aripiprazole should be described as an exploratory finding at high risk of bias, not as evidence of benefit beyond usual care.

key_findings.finding: Design: 165 people with DSM-5 stimulant-induced psychosis randomized 1:1:2 to aripiprazole (42), paliperidone (40) or treatment as usual (83) by opaque sealed envelopes drawn by an independent staff member; months 0 to 12 with outcome assessors blinded, months 12 to 24 open-label with assessors unblinded and participants free to continue or stop their assigned treatment.
key_findings.locator: 2.1 Study design and participants, 1st paragraph; 2.2 Randomization and blinding, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 3.2 Medications and safety, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Participants: mean age 38.69 (SD 10.08), 69.70% men; 89.70% had ever used methamphetamine and 59.39% cocaine; baseline CGI-S 3.33 (1.29) and BPRS-24 29.70 (6.00); 65.63% of baseline urine samples stimulant-positive. The aripiprazole arm had fewer men (45.24% vs 82.50% and 75.90%), was younger (34.36 vs 39.95 and 40.28 years) and had higher BPRS-24 scores (31.55 vs 28.33 on TAU).
key_findings.note: Editors' chi-square for sex across the three arms: 16.5 on 2 df, p < 0.001. The baseline text calls the same 89.70% primary methamphetamine use (reporting issue 13).

key_findings.finding: Usual care was not antipsychotic-free care: 55.43% of the TAU group were antipsychotic-free at baseline, 31.33% at 12 months and 24.10% at 24 months; TAU could include any antipsychotic other than the two study drugs. No participant received structured psychotherapy or drug counselling.
key_findings.locator: 2.3 Medications, 1st paragraph; 3.2 Medications and safety, 1st paragraph; 3 Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome as published (MMRM, change from baseline, contrast with TAU): CGI-S at 12 months aripiprazole −0.55 (95% CI −1.03 to −0.07), p = 0.03, d = −0.31; paliperidone −0.4 (−0.86 to 0.06), p = 0.09. CGI-S at 24 months aripiprazole −0.65 (−1.22 to −0.09), p = 0.03, d = −0.38; paliperidone −0.02 (−0.6 to 0.56). CGI-I and CGI-E improved more than TAU on both drugs at 12 months (for example CGI-E aripiprazole −4.19, d = −1.72; paliperidone −3.3, d = −1.36) and only on aripiprazole at 24 months (CGI-I −0.74, −1.43 to −0.06; CGI-E −4.17, −6.73 to −1.6).
key_findings.note: The 24-month ratings were made without blinding; CGI-I and CGI-E have no baseline.

key_findings.finding: Symptom ratings did not show the same pattern: severity of psychopathology on the BPRS-24 (and stimulant use disorder severity, dependence, executive function, frequency of use and motivation) showed no consistent between-group differences; CGI-S responder rates did not differ (12 months: 70.83%, 75.0%, 64.06%). Aripiprazole had more BPRS-24 responders than TAU at 12 months (16 of 24, 66.67%, vs 19 of 64, 29.69%; p = 0.002), not at 24 months.
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Secondary outcomes, 2nd paragraph; 3.5 Clinical responder analysis, 1st paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: A post hoc review of health records found 28 participants (5 aripiprazole, 11 paliperidone, 12 TAU) with a diagnosis of schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder before enrolment. Without them (137 participants), the 12-month primary effects were attenuated: aripiprazole against TAU, CGI-S p = 0.12 and CGI-I p = 0.07 at 12 months, against p = 0.04 and p = 0.03 at 24 months; CGI-E remained significant at both time points (p < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: 3.6 Conversion from StIP to schizophrenia, 1st paragraph; 3.7 Sensitivity analysis, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The same paragraph first says all 12-month primary outcomes had p > 0.05 and then that CGI-E was significant at 12 months (reporting issue 6).

key_findings.finding: Conversion to schizophrenia (new ICD-10 diagnosis of schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder, attending psychiatrist) among the 137 without an earlier diagnosis: 7 of 137 (5.11%) within 24 months; aripiprazole 3 of 38 (7.89%), paliperidone 2 of 29 (6.89%), TAU 2 of 70 (2.86%); chi-square 1.45 on 2 df, p = 0.48; mean time to conversion 332 days (SD 176.83, range 128 to 611).
key_findings.locator: 3.6 Conversion from StIP to schizophrenia, 1st paragraph; 2.5 Statistical analysis, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: The per-arm numbers do not reconcile with the exclusions (reporting issue 12).

key_findings.finding: Serious adverse events in 4 participants (2.42%): one suicide in the aripiprazole group 6 months after randomization; three paliperidone participants stopped treatment (atrial fibrillation at 3 months, QTc prolongation at 6 months, pneumonia with acute renal failure at 6 months); none on TAU. GASS side-effect scores were mild with no between-group difference; paliperidone had more extrapyramidal side effects at 24 months (chi-square 6.73, p = 0.03) and more weight gain at 12 months (chi-square 11.00, p = 0.004) than TAU.
key_findings.note: The Bonferroni-corrected p for weight gain is printed as 0.0009, smaller than the uncorrected value (reporting issue 4).

key_findings.finding: Exploratory secondary results for paliperidone against TAU at 24 months: stimulant-positive urine 76.47% vs 46.81% (OR 14.51, 95% CI 2.07 to 101.74; printed p < 0.001) and a larger decline on the MoCA (−2.06, −3.28 to −0.85; d = −0.97); also against aripiprazole on the MoCA (−1.57, −2.97 to −0.17).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: the urine OR's interval implies p of about 0.007; the printed percentages (13 of 17 vs 22 of 47) give a crude OR of about 3.7, so the model-based OR is far larger than the raw contrast.

key_findings.finding: Attrition: 70.30% (116 of 165) assessed at 12 months and 53.94% (89 of 165) at 24 months; the sample fell short of the target of 240 because of COVID-19 disruption. The responder denominators imply 57%, 70% and 77% assessed at 12 months on aripiprazole, paliperidone and TAU.
key_findings.note: Arm-level percentages are editors' calculations from Table 3 (24 of 42, 28 of 40, 64 of 83).

key_findings.finding: Registered outcomes: the record first posted on 2 April 2018 (version 7, 26 April 2019, before enrolment began) gave the relative risk of psychosis relapse over 36 months as the primary outcome; it was unchanged in version 13 (4 July 2025), replaced by the BPRS-24 at 12 and 24 months in version 14 (12 November 2025), the same update that shortened every registered time frame from 36 to 24 months, and by the CGI scales at 12 and 24 months in version 15 (23 March 2026); outcome measures changed only in versions 2, 14 and 15. Primary completion was 31 May 2024 and study completion 31 May 2025 (both actual). The registry's exclusion criteria include a diagnosis of schizophrenia; schizoaffective disorder is not named.
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03485417: Record History, version list and versions 7, 13, 14 and 15 (Outcome Measures; comparisons of versions 13 and 14, and 14 and 15); current record, Study Record Dates and Eligibility Criteria

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: a sample about 30% smaller than planned; mostly mild-to-moderate psychosis; heterogeneous usual care and uncontrolled concomitant medication; no placebo group, so the natural course and untreated conversion risk cannot be judged; possible expectation bias in the open-label second year, so the 24-month benefits should be interpreted with caution; 24 months may be too short to characterize progression to schizophrenia.

reporting_issues.issue: The primary outcome was changed after the trial ended. From registration (2018) to version 13 (July 2025) the registered primary outcome was the relative risk of psychosis relapse over 36 months; version 14 (November 2025) made it the BPRS-24 at 12 and 24 months and version 15 (March 2026, two months before submission) the CGI scales, which the article reports as primary. The article does not report relapse or mention the changes, and the secondary outcome of transition to schizophrenia is registered by DSM-5, at 36 months until version 13 and at 24 months from version 14 (the update that shortened every registered time frame and replaced the primary outcome), but reported by ICD-10.
reporting_issues.page: registry record (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03485417, Record History, versions 7, 13, 14 and 15); publisher HTML, 2.4 Outcome assessments and 2.5 Statistical analysis
reporting_issues.consequence: The published primary analysis is effectively post hoc; the CGI results, the only outcomes favouring aripiprazole consistently, cannot be taken as a confirmatory test.

reporting_issues.issue: Twenty-eight of 165 participants (17%) had a diagnosis of schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder before enrolment, found only by a post hoc record review, although the registry excludes people diagnosed with schizophrenia.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, 3.6 Conversion from StIP to schizophrenia, 1st paragraph; registry record, Eligibility Criteria
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample is partly a sample of primary psychotic disorder; the 12-month advantage depended partly on these participants (3.7).

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3 the aripiprazole CGI-I responder rate at 12 months is printed as 15/24 (71.43%); 15 of 24 is 62.5%, and the printed chi-square of 10.76 fits 15 of 24 rather than 15 of 21 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The percentage overstates the aripiprazole responder rate at 12 months; the count and the test statistic are consistent with each other.

reporting_issues.issue: The Bonferroni-corrected p for weight gain on paliperidone is printed as 0.0009, smaller than its uncorrected value (0.004, which matches chi-square 11.00 on 2 df); the extrapyramidal comparison is said to lose significance after correction but is printed with its uncorrected p (0.03).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, 3.2 Medications and safety, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: A Bonferroni correction cannot lower a p value; the corrected values are misreported, although the conclusion (weight gain significant, extrapyramidal effects not) may stand.

reporting_issues.issue: The stimulant-urine odds ratio for paliperidone against TAU is printed as 14.51 (95% CI 2.07 to 101.74) with p < 0.001; the interval implies p of about 0.007 (editors' calculation from the log-scale interval).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor for significance, but the exploratory harm is less certain than the printed p suggests, and the very wide interval reflects few observations.

reporting_issues.issue: The sensitivity-analysis paragraph first states that all primary outcomes at 12 months had p > 0.05, then that CGI-E differences favoured aripiprazole at both 12 and 24 months (p < 0.001).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which 12-month results survive the exclusion of people with earlier schizophrenia is unclear; the numbers are only in Supplementary Table S12 (not read).

reporting_issues.issue: The arms differ at baseline more than expected after randomization: men 45.24% on aripiprazole vs 82.50% and 75.90% (editors' chi-square 16.5 on 2 df, p < 0.001), mean age 34.36 vs 39.95 and 40.28, and higher BPRS-24 and dependence scores on aripiprazole; the analyses adjust only for the baseline value of each outcome.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1; 2.5 Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Either chance or a problem with allocation; residual confounding of the arm comparisons by sex, age and severity cannot be excluded.

reporting_issues.issue: CGI-I and CGI-E have no baseline rating, and the CGI-E rates a treatment's therapeutic effect against its side effects; how it was scored for the 55% of TAU participants taking no antipsychotic is not described. The large CGI-E effect sizes (d about −1.7) are not discussed in this light.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, 2.5 Statistical analysis, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, footnote b; 3.2, 1st paragraph; registry record, Primary Outcome Measures (CGI-E description)
reporting_issues.consequence: The CGI-E contrast may partly measure whether a participant received a study drug rather than how well they were; it should not be cited as an effect size of treatment.

reporting_issues.issue: The BPRS-24 responder criterion (a reduction of at least 50% in total score) is not workable on raw totals when the lowest possible score is 24 (registry) and the baseline mean is 29.70; a correction for the scale minimum is not described.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, 2.5 Statistical analysis, 3rd paragraph; Table 1; registry record, Secondary Outcome Measures (BPRS-24 description)
reporting_issues.consequence: The BPRS-24 responder rates cannot be interpreted without knowing how the reduction was computed.

reporting_issues.issue: The blinding section says independent assessors conducted all outcome ratings, while the outcome-assessment section names three authors as the psychiatrists who rated the CGI scales and BPRS-24, without saying at which visits. The medications section also says the week-1 tolerability re-assessment was made by attending psychiatrists blinded to treatment allocation, although under the randomization procedure the attending psychiatrist received the allocation and prescribed the drug.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, 2.2 Randomization and blinding, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; 2.3 Medications, 1st paragraph; 2.4 Outcome assessments, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether primary-outcome ratings after baseline were made by study authors, and whether they were blind, is unclear; the article's statements about who was blind to allocation do not agree.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor: the abstract describes the participants as adults although eligibility began at age 16 (Methods; registry) and the youngest age enrolled is not given; the QTc value is printed as 472 m (milliseconds intended).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Abstract › Methods; 2.1, 2nd paragraph; 3.2, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: In the conversion analysis, 5, 11 and 12 participants with an earlier diagnosis are excluded from arms of 42, 40 and 83, which leaves 37, 29 and 71, but 38, 29 and 70 are printed (137 in all either way), and the percentages (7.89%, 2.86%) use 38 and 70; the printed counts give a chi-square of about 1.53 on 2 df (p = 0.47), not 1.45 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, 3.6 Conversion from StIP to schizophrenia, 1st paragraph; 3.2 Medications and safety, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the conclusion of no difference between arms is unchanged.

reporting_issues.issue: The baseline text says 89.70% primarily used methamphetamine, but Table 1 gives 148 (89.70%) as lifetime methamphetamine use, with 59.39% lifetime cocaine use and 49.70% lifetime use of both; the share whose primary drug was methamphetamine is not given.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, 3.1 Baseline characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (Methamphetamine use, Cocaine use, Lifetime use of both stimulants)
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample can be described as people who had ever used methamphetamine (about nine in ten), not as people who mainly used it.

reporting_issues.issue: Minor misprints (editors' arithmetic): Table 1 gives ketamine on aripiprazole as 29 (59.05%), where 29 of 42 is 69.05%; detoxification-centre admission on paliperidone as 21 (51.50%), where 21 of 40 is 52.50%; tertiary education as 22 (12.58%), where 22 of 165 is 13.33%; Table 3 gives BPRS-24 responders on usual care at 24 months as 22/50 (44.02%), where 22 of 50 is 44.00%.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML, Table 1 (Ketamine, Detox center admission, Tertiary or above rows); Table 3 (BPRS-24, month 24, TAU)
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the results; percentages should be recomputed from the counts.

disagreements.first_pass: it was unchanged in version 13 (4 July 2025), replaced by the BPRS-24 at 12 and 24 months in version 14 (12 November 2025) and by the CGI scales at 12 and 24 months in version 15 (23 March 2026). Primary completion was 31 May 2024. The registry's exclusion criteria include a diagnosis of schizophrenia. … After the trial ended (primary completion 31 May 2024; study completion 31 May 2025), version 14 (12 November 2025) made the BPRS-24 at 12 and 24 months the primary outcome, and version 15 (23 March 2026) replaced it with the CGI scales at 12 and 24 months, moving the BPRS-24 to secondary. … and the secondary outcome of transition to schizophrenia is registered by DSM-5 at 36 months but reported by ICD-10 at 24 months.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 21: confirmed, with two additions: every outcome time frame stayed at 36 months from version 2 (2018) to version 13 (4 July 2025) and became 24 months only in version 14 (12 November 2025), together with the switch of primary outcome, after actual primary completion (31 May 2024) and actual study completion (31 May 2025), so no 24-month design was registered before the outcome change; the registry's actual study completion is a year after the article's final follow-up, and neither source says whether data were collected after 24 months. The registry names schizophrenia, not schizoaffective disorder, among its exclusions.
disagreements.resolution: Checked in the ClinicalTrials.gov Record History: the version list shows Outcome Measures changed only in versions 2, 14 and 15; the comparison of versions 13 and 14 shows the relapse outcome (36 months) replaced by the BPRS-24 (12 and 24 months) and every secondary time frame moved from 36 to 24 months; the comparison of versions 14 and 15 shows the CGI scales replacing the BPRS-24 as primary; primary completion 2024-05-31 and study completion 2025-05-31, both actual, in versions 13 to 15; the exclusions name schizophrenia only. The article's final follow-up (31 May 2024) is in 3 Results, 1st paragraph. Added to the finding, the registration detail and the outcome-switch issue.
